description: I’m a software developer skilled in React, web UI, Python, and data analysis. I’m interested in using technology to help people, protect the environment, and make education more accessible. For this challenge, I’m building EarthBeat, an interactive experience that transforms NASA Earth visualizations into meaningful sound for blind, low-vision, and visual learners. I plan to work independently, but I’m happy to connect with participants experienced in accessibility, audio, or Earth science.
summary: EarthBeat is an accessible web "Earth Jukebox" that turns a NASA Earth Information Center visualization — Lightning Events Detected from the International Space Station 2017–2023 — into explainable sound in real time. As the NASA video plays, EarthBeat measures every analyzed frame (where the lightning points are, how much of the globe they cover, how strong, spread out and changeable they are) and maps those measurements to stereo position, pitch, rhythm, loudness, tone and soft ticks, the same way every time. A live legend and a screen-reader-friendly summary explain what each sound means. EarthBeat answers the challenge by pairing EIC visual frames with dynamic, data-driven sonification, with accessibility for blind and low-vision users as its core. It matters because Earth science is shared almost only through pictures; EarthBeat lets more people hear patterns such as lightning rising and falling with the seasons.
details:
The problem. NASA's Earth Information Center (EIC) visualizations show how our planet is changing, but they are almost entirely visual. People who are blind or have low vision — and many learners who understand better by listening — cannot reach those patterns. A music track added to a video would not help: the sound must carry the data and explain itself.

What EarthBeat does. EarthBeat is a single-page web app built around NASA's "Lightning Events Detected from the International Space Station (ISS) 2017–2023" (NASA Scientific Visualization Studio, ID 5011). The listener presses Play; the NASA video plays and EarthBeat generates sound from its frames in real time. The experience includes play/pause, restart, seek, 0.5×/1×/1.5× speed, volume, mute, an immediate "Stop sound" (also the Esc key), a gentle-sound mode, switchable sound layers, an activity timeline of the whole video, three guided listening moments, a guided story, a methodology section with live-computed validation, and full sources and credits.

Frame-analysis pipeline. Ten times per second of video, the browser copies the current frame to a canvas and reduces it to 160×90 pixels by repeated halving (so small points are averaged, not skipped). In this visualization each lightning event is drawn as a saturated yellow point, while clouds, stars, labels, the orbit line and the season wheel are white or gray. EarthBeat therefore classifies "lightning-colored" pixels by yellowness (the smaller of red and green minus blue) rather than brightness, and masks the corner that holds the date and season wheel. From the detected pixels it computes normalized 0–1 features: horizontal and vertical position of the activity, share of the frame covered, mean and peak color strength, left/right and upper/lower balance, spatial spread and change since the previous frame. Features are smoothed with short time constants and an on/off hysteresis so pixel noise does not cause chatter.

Sound mapping. Left–right position → stereo position; height in the frame → pitch on an 11-note pentatonic scale (220–880 Hz); coverage → pulse speed (up to 6 notes per second) and the level of a soft background bed; color strength → note loudness; spread → tone brightness; sudden change → a short soft tick. Rhythm advances with video time, so the sound evolves only as the NASA visualization advances and stops when it stops. There is no randomness: the same frames and settings always produce the same notes. The pentatonic scale keeps the result musical while preserving relative order (higher in the frame = higher note); EarthBeat states that notes are not physical units.

Accessibility. No autoplay; sound starts only on Play. Every control is a native, labeled element and works by keyboard; a skip link, landmarks and one heading outline support screen readers. The video has a text description, and a polite live region summarizes the current activity in words about every four seconds (never per frame), which can be turned off. Play, pause, seek position, mute, stop, errors and the end are announced. High-contrast and reduced-motion modes, strong focus outlines, layouts from 360 px phones to desktop, and a gentle-sound mode with a limiter, a 70 Hz high-pass filter and an 880 Hz highest note keep the experience comfortable. Without sound, the live text and legend values still convey every mapping. EarthBeat is designed toward WCAG 2.2 AA practices; automated checks report 0 violations, and the remaining gap — testing with blind and low-vision users — is stated openly.

Technical stack. React 19 and TypeScript (strict), Vite, the native Web Audio API and Canvas 2D; no backend, accounts, analytics or third-party requests. Testing with Vitest and Testing Library (unit/component), Playwright with Google Chrome (browser smoke tests), and axe-core (automated accessibility). FFmpeg was used to make a full-length 720p web copy of the NASA video (nothing cut) and to run the same analysis code offline over the whole video. Hosted on GitHub Pages. Source code: https://github.com/fernandojcardenas/earthbeat

Validity. The source file is documented with its checksum. Two complete offline analysis runs produced identical features. The browser's measurements were compared with the offline measurements at seven points in the video and followed the same pattern. Running the analysis over the whole video shows that the pitch feature tracks the seasons shown on NASA's season wheel: at every northern-summer reading checked, activity sits higher in the frame (height 0.57 or more) than at every northern-winter reading (0.51 or less), so the melody rises in northern summers and falls in northern winters — consistent with the seasonal patterns NASA says the visualization shows. Measured in Chrome, the app's audio output is about five times louder during dense lightning activity than during frames with no lightning, and stays far below full scale. Automated tests confirm bounded values, monotonic mappings, determinism, hard caps on note rate, loudness and simultaneous sounds, and clean stop/mute behavior.

Limitations. EarthBeat analyzes a NASA-rendered video, not the raw Lightning Imaging Sensor archive, so it conveys relative visual patterns, not lightning counts or physical units. Compression, colors, masking, resolution and sampling rate affect the measurements. Left and right are positions in the picture; the globe rotates, so they are not fixed longitudes. The musical scale and smoothing are interpretive choices. EarthBeat is an educational and exploratory tool, not a weather-warning or forecasting product.

Completed during the hackathon. Everything listed above: data processing and validation, the analysis and audio engines, the complete accessible web app, 51 automated tests, documentation, the seven-slide demo and public deployment.

Next steps. Co-design and test EarthBeat with blind and low-vision students and their teachers; apply the same engine to more EIC visualizations (for example sea-surface temperature or vegetation), with a per-visualization color model; and test end to end with VoiceOver and NVDA on phones and computers.

Use of SI-assisted tools. SI-assisted tools supported planning, code, testing and documentation under my direction and review; EarthBeat contains no SI-generated scientific data, imagery, video, narration, voice or music. Full disclosure: SI_DISCLOSURE.md in the repository and the app's Sources section.
